body: The report shows active diplomacy but no convergence, so markets are unlikely to price a settlement soon. European defence stocks are the most headline-sensitive, and any sign of a breakthrough would test their rally. A credible peace path would eventually weigh on European gas prices and diesel cracks, where Russian refining and product exports have been a supply risk, and could support the euro. For oil, the Middle East remains the bigger driver, so Ukraine headlines are a secondary factor for crude itself. Washington has put Ukraine’s NATO membership on the table as a bargaining chip, but Moscow wants the opposite and Berlin isn’t on board, so a deal still looks distant. US envoys have floated the idea of NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for Kyiv ceding territory to Russia, a proposal that would break with long-standing US policy and run directly against Moscow’s demands, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported. According to people familiar with the talks cited by the Journal, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have raised the idea in several conversations with European officials in recent months. Most recently it came up with President Volodymyr Zelensky and European national security advisers at a meeting in Dublin last week. It was also raised in at least one meeting in the United Arab Emirates involving Ukrainian, European and Russian negotiators. The US has put two scenarios on the table, the report said. The first would see Ukraine give up the part of the Donbas region it still controls in return for full NATO membership. The second would freeze the conflict along the current front line, leaving some of the Donbas in Ukrainian hands, with security guarantees provided through a treaty with the US and possibly European allies. A US official said many ideas are under discussion and that both Ukraine and Russia would have to agree to any final deal. It is unclear how seriously the idea is being pursued, or whether President Donald Trump has changed his view. He ruled out Ukrainian NATO membership early last year as unacceptable to Russia. Zelensky confirmed the question had been raised, recounting that the Americans asked, “What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?” He has said repeatedly that Ukraine will not give up its land, and that any deal would need approval from the Ukrainian people. Moscow’s position points the other way. In a non-paper seen by the Journal, Russian negotiators demanded that Ukraine remove its NATO aspirations from its constitution, that the alliance commit not to station troops or equipment in Ukraine, and that Western arms deliveries stop. They also called for NATO to roll back military infrastructure in Eastern Europe to 1997 levels. European negotiators described the demands as maximalist opening bids. Divisions within NATO add a further hurdle, since the alliance can only expand by consensus. French President Emmanuel Macron said after talks in Berlin on Thursday that it was time to discuss Ukraine’s membership. German officials were unwilling to pursue it, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz has told aides he does not expect Ukraine to join in his lifetime. Kushner said separately that Russia had become comfortable with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine. For markets, the report is a reminder that peace talks are active but far from a deal. Any credible move toward a settlement would be watched closely in European defence stocks, European gas prices and the euro, and in oil product markets, where Russian refining and export flows have been a source of supply risk. With Russia and Ukraine still far apart on core issues, those markets are likely to treat individual headlines with caution. Your market education doesn't end here. body: The rates message (like this: J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call ) is hitting the whole crypto complex, not just Bitcoin. Ether dropped below $1,800 and sentiment gauges sit at extremes. Spot ETF products traded lower with the underlying, and IBIT and FBTC each fell less than 1% on the day. That leaves crypto equities such as COIN and MSTR, and listed miners, exposed to both falling token prices and a weaker tech tape. Bitcoin is trading as a high-beta risk asset rather than a hedge, so equity volatility and Fed pricing remain the main drivers for now. Bitcoin is trading like a leveraged bet on Fed policy, and Thursday’s mix of hawkish minutes and a stock market rout pushed it to a four-month low. Bitcoin fell to around $61,600 on Thursday, its lowest level since early July. The move came as a 1,000-point drop in the Dow and fresh talk of tighter Federal Reserve policy pushed investors out of riskier assets. The token was down a little over 2% on the day by early evening in New York, leaving it within reach of the $60,000 mark and roughly half its record high. The selling tracked Wall Street closely. Bitcoin traded near $63,900 at the US open and slipped to around $62,250 by lunchtime, while the Dow shed more than 1,000 points and the VIX volatility gauge climbed above 28. A short-seller report on AMD added to pressure on tech stocks. Ether dropped below $1,800, and the widely watched Fear and Greed Index sat at 10, deep in extreme fear territory. Rates are the bigger backdrop. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting, released on Wednesday, showed most officials favour further increases, with some open to a half-point move in December. The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% in October, with two dissenters preferring a quarter-point hike. Since then, a hotter-than-expected October inflation report has met the threshold Governor Christopher Waller had set out for when a 50 basis point increase might be warranted. Higher rates raise the cost of holding assets that pay no yield, and Bitcoin has been absorbing that message for weeks. It is on course for a seventh straight weekly loss, a run that has taken it from about $87,500 in early October. Flows offer little support. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw more than $300 million in net outflows on Wednesday, taking November’s total to roughly $2.6 billion, and analysts also point to miners selling into a thinning market. Traders will watch whether the $60,000 level holds, Thursday’s ETF flow data for any sign that redemptions are slowing, and incoming US data ahead of the Fed’s December meeting. A run of softer numbers could cool hike expectations quickly. Another hot print would likely keep the pressure on. Your market education doesn't end here. body: The disclosure adds to political pressure for tighter China chip rules, a risk for Nvidia and AMD’s China revenue at a time when AI and semiconductor shares are already being sold hard across Asia. Nvidia saying it has stopped H200 shipments limits the near-term earnings hit, but any formal tightening would also weigh on Chinese AI developers’ access to computing power. Hong Kong-listed Tencent, Alibaba and Baidu are the most exposed names on the Chinese side. The story also keeps Washington’s broader export-control push in focus, including reported plans to curb advanced chip exports to parts of Southeast Asia. Washington’s own licensing data show it cleared hundreds of thousands of AI chips for Chinese firms, including military-listed ones, handing China hawks fresh ammunition just as Nvidia says it has stopped shipping. The US Commerce Department approved shipments of about 880,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026, according to licensing data released on Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee. The approvals covered Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X. They included 150,000 chips for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD. All four companies appear on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed firms, and together they account for just over 30% of the approved total. Companies had sought permission to ship more than 3.4 million chips over the period, so roughly a quarter of requested volumes were approved. It is not clear how many of the approvals turned into actual deliveries. Nvidia said the licences came with strict conditions and limited volumes and that “we have since stopped shipping H200s to China.” AMD said it complies with US export control laws. Reuters reported in May that about 10 Chinese companies had been cleared to buy the H200 but no deliveries had been made. A Commerce official later told the committee that shipments had begun but there had been very few. The Commerce Department said its H200 licensing follows a January 2026 rule that adds significant national security requirements for applicants, allowing case-by-case review rather than a presumption of denial. Critics are unconvinced. A former US official who specialises in US-China technology policy called the share going to military-listed firms astonishing and questioned whether Commerce had carried out a serious security review. The release is unusual. Committee Chair Brian Mast described it as the most detailed public disclosure since the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 expanded Commerce’s powers over sensitive technology exports. It comes as the Trump administration faces closer scrutiny of its China chip policy following reports involving former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, which have revived calls in Washington for a tougher stance. The policy backdrop has swung sharply. The Biden administration restricted Chinese access to advanced AI chips over concerns they would strengthen China’s military and erode the US lead in AI. President Trump reversed course in December 2025, allowing Nvidia to ship the H200 to China. With pressure building on both sides of the political divide, investors will watch for any move to tighten licensing again. That would weigh on chipmakers’ China revenue and on Chinese tech firms’ access to advanced computing. Your market education doesn't end here. summary: Canada is building an energy export industry for a world beyond the tariff-chasing United States. In 2024, the U.S. bought all but 0.01% of Canada’s natural gas exports. body: Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. Canada is building an energy export industry for a world beyond the tariff-chasing United States. In 2024, the U.S. bought all but 0.01% of Canada’s natural gas exports. Ottawa now wants 55% of those exports to go to other countries by the mid-2030s, and Germany’s state-owned Uniper has signed a 20-year deal for liquefied natural gas from a planned British Columbia terminal. Prime Minister Mark Carney has fast-tracked a state-backed pipeline to carry 1 million barrels a day of Alberta crude to the Pacific coast for Asian buyers, and Alberta has cut royalties on new oil sands projects to 2% to double output by 2035. Carney took that strategy to Shenzhen this week for the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which opened on Wednesday with leaders and business executives from 21 member economies. He met Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday and spoke briefly with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines on Wednesday. Afterward, Carney’s office said the two had discussed “the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement.” Trump is set to hold a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, where the White House says he will discuss reducing nuclear weapons. The brief meeting with Trump is unlikely to thaw trade tensions between the two neighbours or change Canada’s new energy trajectory. Trump has targeted Canada with sweeping tariffs and public criticism throughout his second term, turning a trade dispute into a broader diplomatic fight. In August, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on roughly US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, with 50% tariffs on Canadian cars, auto parts and steel set to take effect on January 1, 2027. Carney has answered with retaliatory tariffs while pursuing trade deals elsewhere, including with China. Related: 5 Oil and Gas Stocks That Crushed Third-Quarter Earnings Estimates In Tuesday’s meeting, Carney and Xi expanded their bilateral trade agreement , which has restored market access for more than 90% of Canadian exports previously hit by Chinese tariffs. China agreed to remove or reduce tariffs on about $400 million in additional Canadian exports, including frozen pork and seafood. Canada extended existing tariff exemptions on certain Chinese steel and aluminum products for another two years and added relief for 32 more steel and aluminum items in short supply domestically. The two leaders also discussed cooperation in oil and gas, and Canadian exports to China rose almost 40% in the first nine months of the year. Canada is also working to attract the capital it needs to build energy infrastructure and reduce its reliance on the U.S. market. Last week, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s government introduced a 10-year preferential royalty framework for new oil sands developments and expansions. Projects that add at least 5,000 barrels per day will pay a 2% gross revenue royalty for their first five years of production, rising by one percentage point a year to 6% in years nine and ten. The framework is designed to help the province double output to 8 million barrels per day by 2035. Alberta estimates that reaching that target could generate about 205 billion Canadian dollars in additional government revenue by 2040 and more than $1.3 trillion by 2060. Smith said in March that Asian and Middle Eastern investors, including sovereign wealth funds, were willing to take 15% to 30% stakes in a new West Coast pipeline. The United States remains by far the biggest buyer of Canadian energy, taking 90.8% of Canada’s hydrocarbon exports by volume through decades of integrated cross-border pipelines and power grids. Last year, Canada shipped 3.9 million barrels per day of crude to the U.S., supplying 63.4% of total U.S. crude imports. body: Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… Bank of Montreal (BMO) is jumping back into U.S. oil and gas investment banking six years after abandoning the business, apparently finding the American energy sector considerably more attractive now that companies are spending billions buying up each other. BMO Capital Markets is hiring Ali Akbar from Mizuho Financial Group to lead its rebuilt U.S. energy practice, Reuters reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the plans. Other Mizuho bankers are expected to join him next year. Akbar specializes in pipelines and other midstream infrastructure. BMO exited U.S. oil and gas investment banking in late 2020, when pandemic lockdowns had devastated petroleum demand, crude prices briefly turned negative, and dozens of American energy companies filed for bankruptcy. American energy companies are spending billions on acquisitions. Just this week, Diamondback Energy agreed to pay approximately $5 billion in cash and stock for Double Eagle's remaining interest in a Midland Basin partnership. Deals like this generate business for investment banks by advising buyers and sellers, arranging financing, and underwriting securities. BMO's return is about investment banking only and should not be mistaken for a reversal of some wholesale abandonment of fossil fuels. In fact, BMO’s overall fossil fuel financing increased 25% between 2020 and 2021, reaching $23.5 billion, according to figures published by Investors for Paris Compliance. The bank also revised its coal policy in November 2023, removing a statement that restricted coal financing amid scrutiny from West Virginia over financial institutions accused of boycotting energy companies. BMO's latest move doesn't necessarily mean the bank will increase direct lending to oil producers, but it is a clear sign that BMO sees enough prospective business in American oil, gas, and pipeline transactions to justify rebuilding an entire team it dismantled six years ago. body: What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… Exxon’s success is reigniting Big Oil’s appetite for high-risk frontier exploration, demonstrating the potential rewards of long-term investment in new oil discoveries. Oil majors are expanding exploration across South America, Africa and Asia, seeking to replicate Guyana’s success as geopolitical disruptions reinforce the importance of new supplies. Exxon announced this week that total oil production in Guyana had topped 1 million barrels. Guyana’s transformation into a formidable oil power is now motivating other oil majors to seek opportunities to replicate Exxon’s story. It is quite easy to see why. Exxon, along with its partners Hess Corp. and CNOOC, spent billions on developing the Stabroek Block offshore the tiny South American country. The investment paid off with a string of discoveries opening up resources estimated at over 11 billion barrels of crude. With this year’s massive supply disruption because of the war between the United States and Israel, and Iran, Guyana turned into an even bigger star in Exxon’s portfolio, boosting profits. The Financial Times noted in a report this week that Exxon’s Guyana bet, which began back in 1999, when the company acquired the Stabroek Block, went against the mainstream in the industry. Active exploration offshore Guyana began in the late 2000s, and in 2015, Exxon, Hess, and CNOOC struck their first oil. But 2015 was also the year of the Paris Agreement and what many saw as a turning tide moving away from oil and gas and into alternative, low-carbon energy. Related: 5 Oil and Gas Stocks That Crushed Third-Quarter Earnings Estimates Over the past decade, the green investment movement gathered momentum, prompting oil and gas companies to make investor reward a top priority, pushing exploration and growth to the back seat. Not Exxon, however. Exxon was spending billions in Guyana and drilling for more oil when pretty much every forecasting outlet was saying peak oil demand was nigh. The forecasts have yet to come true, while this year the world got a stark reminder of just how vital crude oil and natural gas are for the proper functioning of any economy, including the greenest--the European Union’s oil and gas imports did not slump as a result of the Middle East disruption. They moved slightly lower while soaring in value because of the oil and gas price shock. “It was the textbook definition of right place, right time. It became one of the crown jewels of ExxonMobil’s repositioning, demonstrating that the company could still deliver enormous resource additions and highly competitive barrels,” Rystad Energy analyst Schreiner Parker told the Financial Times. Yet there is more to the story than just the right place and right time. It was the willingness to risk billions in investment on oil when everyone was saying oil was on its way out--and do it fast, no less. “What is particularly remarkable is the speed of development: going from first oil in 2019 to more than 1mn barrels per day in just seven years, a feat seemingly only doable by ExxonMobil. Guyana has gone from an exploration success to one of the most important pillars of ExxonMobil’s global upstream growth strategy,” Rystad’s Parker also told the FT. No wonder, then, that other Big Oil majors are looking to frontier regions for a production boost and spending on exploration again instead of divesting oil and gas assets to buy solar and battery businesses. They already did that, and it did not pay off as expected. Now, Big Oil is back to what Big Oil does best: oil and gas. A lot of them are doing it in other parts of South America, the FT’s report noted. Suriname, Guyana’s neighbor, is an obvious choice, but the industry is also expanding in legacy oil producers such as Brazil and Argentina. Japan core inflation soars to highest this year as energy subsidy expiry pushes up consumer prices
summary: The core inflation figure — which strips out prices of food — was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists.
body: Core inflation in Japan soared to a fresh high in 2026, coming in at 2.2% in October as higher energy costs and their knock-on effects pushed up prices in the wider economy. Core inflation, which strips out prices of food, was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists, but was higher than the 2.1% in prior month. Headline inflation came in at 2.3% compared with September's 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which strips out prices of fresh food and energy, dipped slightly to 2.2% from 2.4% in the month before, government data released on Friday showed. Energy subsidies for households expired in September, exposing consumers to higher prices brought about by the Iran war. Energy prices climbed 2.2% in October, a sharp spike from the 0.6% decline in September. Gas prices jumped 5.8% compared to the 2.4% rise the month before. Fuel, light and water charges also saw a considerable acceleration, increasing 3.4% compared to last month's 0.8%. Following the release, the Nikkei 225 index was down 2.1%, while the 10-year JGB yield fell 2 basis points to 2.805%. Japan has reportedly approved reintroduction of energy subsidies in December to stave off higher imported energy prices as higher prices crimp growth, hitting consumption and net exports. The October inflation reading is likely to push the Bank of Japan toward another rate hike in December, despite an unexpected contraction in economic growth in the third quarter. Data from LSEG indicates that there is a 72% chance of a 25 basis point hike from the Bank of Japan. On Wednesday, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament that the central bank was also "mindful" of the weak yen and rising crude prices, saying that these could hurt ⁠households' real income and weigh on consumption more than expected. The yen marginally strengthened to trade at 159.59 against the dollar after the data release. Japan's inflation is likely to still stay above 2% for the rest of 2026 and into the first quarter of 2027, according to Ma Tieying, senior economist at DBS Group Research. She pointed out that while higher energy prices and yen weakness have contributed to headline inflation, the recent upturn is also supported by domestic factors. "Wage growth has remained above 3% for nine consecutive months, pointing to a broader pickup in underlying inflation as stronger wage gains feed through to services prices and household spending. This suggests a more durable wage–price cycle is taking hold." Ma expects the BOJ to raise rates in its December meeting, then twice more in 2027, bringing its terminal rate to 2%.

body: Gold buyers are finally showing some resistance after an extended decline. Improving price action near $3,766 and a recovery toward $3,780 offer encouraging clues, but a sustained move toward $3,800 may be needed before the recovery becomes more convincing. Gold futures are beginning to show something that has been missing during much of their recent decline: selling pressure is no longer consistently producing lasting lower prices. Buyers have made some encouraging progress, but there is still a substantial difference between identifying a possible bottom and confirming a bullish reversal. The latest intraday evidence provides a practical framework for evaluating that difference. Market snapshot: November 18, 2026, approximately 4:29 a.m. US Eastern time. Analysis based on December 2026 Micro Gold futures (MGC), with gold near $3,780.60. All prices below refer to that observation, not continuously updated quotations. Gold recovered from an observed intraday low near $3,759.50 , climbing back into an important area where much of the session's trading activity had previously taken place. The lower boundary of that developing value area was around $3,766.20. For readers unfamiliar with volume-based analysis, a value area represents a range where a substantial portion of trading volume has occurred. Its boundaries can help traders assess whether the market is accepting or rejecting a particular price region. Gold initially moved back above that boundary, briefly slipped beneath it again, and subsequently recovered. What makes the sequence interesting is that buyers did not surrender all their progress during subsequent pullbacks. Instead, the shorter-term price structure began retaining higher prices. The recovery eventually extended toward $3,780, accompanied by improving buying participation and upward price progress. This suggests sellers may be losing some of their earlier effectiveness. However, stronger buying in a short-term recovery does not automatically mean the broader bearish trend has ended. These are reference levels, not automatic buy or sell instructions. VWAP, its deviation bands and the developing value area can move as trading continues. At the latest observation, gold was trading above its first lower VWAP standard-deviation band, located around $3,777.60. VWAP, or volume-weighted average price, measures the average traded price weighted by volume. A market trading below VWAP has generally been transacting beneath that average. Recovering toward it can be meaningful, particularly after an extended period of weakness. For the bullish case, maintaining prices around $3,777-$3,780 would be encouraging. If pullbacks repeatedly find buyers around this region, the recovery could gradually become more convincing. But what if gold briefly holds this area and subsequently falls back toward $3,766? That would not automatically establish another bearish trend leg. It would mean traders need to reassess whether the market can defend its earlier recovery. An important educational lesson is that support and resistance are areas to observe, not magical lines that guarantee a reaction. The developing VWAP was near $3,800-$3,801 during the observation. This creates two potentially interesting situations, depending on whether a trader is already participating in the recovery or is still waiting. For somebody who entered a long position at lower prices, approaching VWAP could provide an opportunity to consider taking partial profits. That is not mandatory. It depends on the original entry, position size, risk and trading plan. title: Anthropic’s blockbuster float signals AI cash - but not a funding boom for all - Small Caps
body: Anthropic’s record float shows there is money for AI, but its retreat from the opening trade suggests Australian software companies should not count on investor Anthropic’s record float shows there is money for AI, but its retreat from the opening trade suggests Australian software companies should not count on investors funding every AI ambition on generous terms. Anthropic briefly reached a valuation of A$3tn when its shares began trading, before retreating off earlier session highs. The developer of Claude nevertheless closed its first session 17% above the offer price, with a US$1.27tn market capitalisation. That is a powerful result for Anthropic as it raises capital to pursue AI growth, despite facing significant uncertainty as a result of it's very large future committed funding requirements and slowing revenue growth. Anthropic has the scale to explain the demand. Its filing records US$33.2bn of revenue in the nine months to September 2026, alongside a heavy operating loss. The company also cautions that its recent revenue growth may not continue at comparable rates. The spending commitments are just as important as the sales. Anthropic has committed to spending substantial sums under its Microsoft contract, regardless of actual usage. Its separate, conditional private placement is backed by Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC Partners. Those proposed investments sit alongside the public offer, rather than forming part of its proceeds. We think the lesson is selective capital, not a universal AI premium. Investors have backed a business with substantial revenue, but that revenue comes with formidable future costs. The market has priced in a very heavy premium on Anthropic, and with OpenAI potentially hitting the boards early next year, there is a question of where continued funding will come from. The strongest counterargument is that a record float can draw more money into technology broadly. Investors who miss out on Anthropic shares, including Australian applicants whose allocations are determined by their brokers, may look elsewhere for exposure. That could improve funding conditions for smaller software businesses as well as large AI developers. The recent fall in the price of Bitcoin may indicate a general rotation out of crypto into the AI trade. However, past history suggests that there will be cheaper entry points available into Anthropic. The previous record holder was SpaceX, whose share later traded below their offer price not long after floating. Abundant initial demand and selective subsequent investing can coexist; especially where early VC investors need to provide returns for their investors. Domestically, all eyes will continue on Firmus and domestic data centre operators like NextDC (ASX:NXT) that have not shared the same recent enthusiasm of US markets. Firmus spectacularly pulled it's IPO back in October after trying to re-cut the book to save the deal, and NextDC has seen it's share price collapse from just under $15 in mid August to just above $5 a share in October. It has subsequently bounced back to around $10. The ASX small-cap stories that matter, filed before 9am AEST. Curated by the Small Caps desk.

title: Anthropic IPO 'exactly what the markets need', but analysts warn of volatility - CNBC
body: Anthropic's blockbuster IPO on Thursday gave markets a much-needed boost after weeks of weakness, though analysts warned that the stock could remain volatile in the coming weeks. Share of the Claude maker opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17 per share, 17% above the IPO price. The offering raised $81.3 billion through the sale of 980 million shares — surpassing SpaceX's June listing to become the largest IPO on record . Nomura strategist Charlie McElligott described investors as "foaming at the mouth" for the offering, with allocations "impossibly low," underscoring the strength of demand. "Anthropic's IPO is exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment," said Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at Walser Wealth Management, adding that markets have been "depressed with all of the negativity in the AI complex over the past several weeks." While the initial pop was not surprising for such a highly anticipated listing, investors should avoid "chasing the IPO," Walser said. She expects the stock to come under pressure in the coming weeks as former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang testifies before the U.S. Senate , potentially reviving concerns around the AI sector. U.S. equities fell sharply on Thursday, with the tech heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% to end at 23,879.20, S&P 500 down 2.02% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 2.19%. Artificial intelligence and technology stocks initially rose thanks to the IPO, but the gains faded as "profit-taking spread across AI-related stocks," said Tiger Brokers chief market strategist James Ooi. "The shares remain highly volatile," said Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan. Walser said that any weakness around the testimony could offer an entry point for investors interested in Anthropic, adding that she remains bullish on the OpenAI rival over the long term. "For investors, it's going to become a blue-chip stock like Google," Ross Gerber, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management told CNBC. He added that U.S. technology valuations are at ridiculously low levels relative to the "crazy amazing innovation" coming out of California. Morningstar's Khan struck a more cautious tone, warning investors against getting swept up in the enthusiasm around Anthropic, advising them instead to step back and "carefully" assess the company as a long-term business. That will depend on Anthropic's ability to scale enterprise adoption, continue improving its models and turn those capabilities into economically useful products and services in the AI ecosystem, he said. "We remain confident that the firm will be able to execute on all three fronts," Khan added, setting a $92 fair value estimate for the stock. Walser stated that Anthropic is "extremely important for the overall AI story" as the first non-Chinese large language model developer to go public. Its listing gives public-market investors their first direct test of how a major standalone AI model developer will be valued and perform outside the chip sector. Meanwhile, rival OpenAI could follow with an IPO sometime in 2027. "This IPO is the show me moment for the AI story," Walser said, as much of the stock market's AI narrative has so far centered on chipmakers.
